name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
summary: The receiving funeral home in Saint Kitts and Nevis files the departure documents with the Ministry of Health (Chief Medical Officer, via the Basseterre Health Centre), which issues a letter permitting the remains to be shipped in. The body must be embalmed and placed in a hermetically sealed container inside an all-wood outer shipping case.
documents: Death certificate (original or certified copy; the London High Commission asks for the original)
Statement of death
Burial / transit permit from the place of death
Embalming certificate or embalmer's affidavit
Letter of non-contagious disease (free from infection) from the local health authority
Coffin sealing certificate
Funeral home letter: only remains in the casket, hermetically sealed container in an all-wood outer case, consignee name and contacts, flight details and arrival time
Proof of identity / citizenship of the deceased (passport bio page or birth certificate)
Copies notarised (London High Commission guidance)
coffin: The body must be in a hermetically sealed container placed inside an all-wood outer shipping container, and a coffin sealing certificate is required. The sealing is done and certified by the funeral home at departure; no witnessing by a Kittitian official is described.
embalming: Embalming is required: an embalming certificate (or embalmer's affidavit) is part of the file.
consular: Documents go to a Saint Kitts and Nevis mission (the Toronto consulate asks for them at least 14 days before departure; the London High Commission asks for notarised copies sent to the local funeral director). On receipt, the Chief Medical Officer issues a letter permitting the remains to be shipped into the Federation. No Strasbourg laissez-passer arrangement applies.
arrival: The person accompanying the remains presents the original documents on arrival and all contents must be declared to Customs. The local funeral director, who processed the file with the Ministry of Health, collects the casket. No legal burial deadline was found in official sources.
private_aviation: No rules specific to private flights were found. The Chief Medical Officer's permission letter must be issued before departure and the casket must clear Customs at a port of entry; the flight details and arrival time are part of the file, so give the exact private flight details to the funeral home.
private_jet_note: Get the Chief Medical Officer's permission letter before take-off; flight details are part of the file.
export: Leaving Saint Kitts and Nevis: the death is registered with the Registrar General (St Kitts) or Registrar General Department (Nevis); the certificate (English, with cause of death) is usually issued within 2 days of a post-mortem. The local funeral director provides the embalming certificate and a permit to transfer the remains. Post-mortems are common for foreign nationals and can take 3-5 days or more because the medical examiner is based in Barbados.
export_points: Death registered with the Registrar General; certificate usually within 2 days of post-mortem
Post-mortem can take 3-5+ days (examiner based in Barbados)
Local funeral director provides embalming certificate and transfer permit
Cremation available locally (Liamuiga Funeral Home)

at_a_glance.consular: File sent to a Kittitian mission
at_a_glance.arrival: Declare to Customs; local funeral home collects

name: Montserrat
summary: Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory with its own health and customs laws; the UK's own rules do not apply on entry. No official published procedure for bringing a casket into Montserrat was found; arrange it through a local funeral home and confirm requirements with the Ministry of Health and Social Services (Environmental Health Department) in advance.
documents: Death certificate (English or translated) - expected, not confirmed
Certificate of cause of death / non-contagious disease certificate - expected, not confirmed
Embalming certificate - expected, not confirmed
Transit / removal permit from the place of death - expected, not confirmed
Confirm the exact list with the Montserrat Ministry of Health and Social Services
coffin: Not published. A hermetically sealed casket in an outer shipping case is the norm in the region and is required by most airlines; confirm with the Environmental Health Department.
embalming: Not published; embalming is expected in practice. Confirm with the Ministry of Health and Social Services.
consular: Montserrat is a UK Overseas Territory: there is no Montserrat consulate abroad. Contact the Government of Montserrat (Ministry of Health and Social Services, tel +1 664 491 2880/2881) directly; British consulates abroad do not issue entry permits for Montserrat.
arrival: The Environmental Health Department carries out port public health surveillance; customs clearance applies at the port of entry. Who issues the import clearance and any burial deadline are not published.
private_aviation: Montserrat's only airport (John A. Osborne) has a very short runway served by small turboprops; most business jets cannot land there, so a casket often travels by small aircraft or ferry via Antigua. Confirm aircraft suitability and port health/customs presence before planning.
private_jet_note: Very short runway: most jets cannot land; plan a transfer via Antigua.
export: No official procedure for sending a body out of Montserrat was found. In practice the local funeral home obtains the death registration, embalming and a removal/transit permit; the Ministry of Health and Social Services should be consulted. The UK requirements for arrival in the UK apply on the receiving side.
export_points: Procedure not published; confirm with the Ministry of Health and Social Services
Local funeral home arranges registration, embalming and transit papers
Transfer usually via Antigua because of the small airport

name: Guadeloupe
summary: Guadeloupe is a French overseas department: French rules apply. A casket coming from abroad needs a transport authorisation from the French embassy or consulate in the country of death, and for air transport the body must be in an airtight metal-lined coffin.
documents: Local death certificate (transcription into French civil status advised, done by the consulate)
Medical certificate / non-contagious disease certificate as required by the departure country
Embalming (soins de conservation) certificate where required at departure
Authorisation to transport the body issued by the French embassy or consulate (or a mortuary laissez-passer from a Strasbourg Agreement state)
Coffin closing / sealing report
Receiving funeral director and burial or cremation arrangements in Guadeloupe
coffin: For any air transport an airtight coffin is mandatory under French rules (in practice a soldered zinc lining inside a wooden coffin). A hermetic coffin cannot normally be cremated without being reopened, so plan cremation before departure.
embalming: France does not impose embalming on every incoming body; it is normally required by the departure country and by carriers for long journeys. Confirm with the consulate.
consular: The French embassy or consulate in the country of death issues the authorisation to transport the body to France (including overseas departments) and can transcribe the death certificate. France is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement, so a laissez-passer from another party state is accepted. From mainland France, no consulate is involved: the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed authorises transport to Guadeloupe.
arrival: The receiving funeral director in Guadeloupe takes charge on arrival after customs and health formalities. French law sets a 14-day limit for burial or cremation; for deaths abroad the official guidance counts it from the body's entry into mainland France, so confirm with the prefecture of Guadeloupe how it is applied for direct arrivals in Guadeloupe.
private_aviation: Same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The airtight zinc-lined coffin rule applies to any flight. Use an airport with customs (the main international airport) and arrange for the funeral director to meet the aircraft.
private_jet_note: Airtight zinc-lined coffin mandatory on any flight into France, including overseas departments.
export: To send a coffin out of Guadeloupe, the funeral director obtains authorisation from the prefect of Guadeloupe (the department where the coffin is closed), for EU, non-EU and mainland France destinations alike. An airtight metal coffin is mandatory for air transport. The destination country's consular requirements also apply.
export_points: Prefect of Guadeloupe authorises transport
Airtight metal-lined coffin mandatory by air
Same prefect authorisation for transport to mainland France
Check the destination consulate's requirements

name: Dominica
summary: No official published procedure for bringing a casket into Dominica was found. Work through a Dominica funeral home, which deals with the Ministry of Health (Environmental Health) and Customs, and expect embalming and a sealed casket with a full set of departure documents.
documents: Death certificate - expected, not confirmed
Certificate of cause of death / non-contagious disease certificate - expected, not confirmed
Embalming certificate - expected, not confirmed
Transit / removal permit from the place of death - expected, not confirmed
Confirm the list with a Dominica consulate or the Ministry of Health
coffin: Not published. A hermetically sealed casket in an outer case is standard in the region and required by most airlines; confirm locally.
embalming: Not published for entry; embalming is expected in practice.
consular: No official consular procedure was found online. Ask the Dominica High Commission or consulate in the country of death whether documents must be authenticated.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at the port of entry; the local funeral home collects. No official burial deadline found. Dominica has no crematorium.
private_aviation: No private-flight rules were found. Use an airport of entry with customs and arrange for the funeral home to meet the aircraft; confirm the entry clearance before take-off.
export: Leaving Dominica: the death is registered at the Registry Department (births, marriages and deaths); a post-mortem is usually carried out for all deaths, usually within four days. If no death certificate can be issued (for example during a police investigation), the police issue a permissive warrant allowing repatriation. The local funeral director provides the certificate of embalming and the permit to transfer the remains. There is no crematorium: cremation requires transfer to Barbados or Saint Lucia.

Post-mortem usual, normally within about 4 days

name: Saint Lucia
summary: Saint Lucia's Public Health (Transportation of Human Remains) Regulations require the cause-of-death certificate, a preparer's statement and a transit permit, a hermetically sealed impervious coffin, and clearance from an environmental health officer before the remains leave the port of entry.
documents: Official certificate of cause of death from the registrar of deaths or similar authority
Statement by the person who prepared the remains, certified by an appropriate authority, describing the preparation and confirming the coffin holds only the body, clothing and packing
Transit permit from the competent authority at the place of death, stating the deceased's names and age
Documents in the official language (English) of Saint Lucia
Environmental health officer's clearance at the port of entry
coffin: Remains must be placed in a hermetically sealed impervious coffin; an outer wooden box or special fabric may be added for protection. Alternatively an embalmed body may be sealed in a plastic container placed in a non-impervious coffin. A durable plaque on the outside must show the name, age and final destination.
embalming: The law allows either thorough disinfection (orifices packed, body wrapped in a disinfectant sheet) in an impervious coffin, or arterial and cavity embalming. Embalming is mandatory if the deceased had a quarantinable disease.
consular: No consular legalisation step is set out in the regulations; documents must be in English. Ask the Saint Lucia mission in the country of death whether authentication is expected.
arrival: Human remains may not leave the port of entry until an environmental health officer issues clearance (prescribed form). Copies of the documents must travel with the remains or reach the environmental health officer within 24 hours. The local funeral director collects. No legal burial deadline found.
pouch: Not accepted on its own: an embalmed body sealed in a plastic container must still be placed in a coffin.
private_aviation: No private-flight rules found. Land at a port of entry where an environmental health officer can issue the clearance; arrange it in advance, especially outside office hours.
private_jet_note: Remains cannot leave the airport until an environmental health officer clears them.
export: Leaving Saint Lucia: the death is registered at the Registry of Civil Status; the certificate (English, with cause of death) is usually issued within 2 days of the post-mortem, which is usually within a week. The same regulations apply to anyone transporting remains: documents go to the Chief Medical Officer, a fee of EC$250 is paid to the Accountant General, and the Chief Medical Officer's certificate must appear on the outside of the coffin.
export_points: Chief Medical Officer certifies the coffin; certificate fixed on the outside
Transport fee EC$250 to the Accountant General
Hermetically sealed impervious coffin with name plaque
Post-mortem usually within a week; certificate within 2 days after

name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
summary: Bodies for burial must arrive in a hermetically sealed impervious coffin with an embalming certificate, an official cause-of-death certificate and a non-contagious disease certificate, all originals. The SVG official responsible for entry of human remains must be told the arrival time and flight in advance.
documents: Official certificate of the cause of death (original)
Certificate that the deceased did not have a contagious disease at death (original)
Embalming certificate (original)
Passport or official ID of the deceased
coffin: Hermetically sealed impervious coffin required for burial. No official witnessing of the sealing is described.
embalming: Required: an embalming certificate must be presented to the officials in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
consular: The SVG High Commission guidance asks for originals of all documents; no legalisation step is described. Many routings transit Barbados, so that country's transit requirements must also be checked.
arrival: The official in SVG responsible for entry of human remains must be given the arrival time and flight number and advises on charges. The local funeral home collects after clearance. No legal burial deadline found.
private_aviation: No rules specific to private flights found. A direct private flight avoids the usual transhipment via Barbados; still give the SVG entry official the flight details and arrival time in advance and land at an airport of entry.
private_jet_note: Notify the SVG official for human remains of the flight and arrival time.
export: Leaving SVG: the death is registered at the Civil Registry (Kingstown or the district); copies take about 2 days. A magistrate issues the medical warrant and, after a post-mortem, the warrant to bury. The local funeral director provides the embalming certificate, transit documents and permission to transfer the remains.

name: Barbados

embalming: Not published for entry; embalming is expected in practice.
consular: No official consular procedure was found online. Contact the Barbados High Commission or consulate in the country of death. Barbados is often a transit point for remains bound for neighbouring islands.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at the port of entry; the local funeral director collects. No official burial deadline found.

name: Grenada
summary: Grenada's Human Remains (Importation Control) Regulations require a cause-of-death certificate, a certified preparer's statement and a transit permit. The body must be embalmed (or fully disinfected) and placed in an impervious, hermetically sealed coffin, or embalmed in a sealed plastic container or air disaster bag.
documents: Official certificate of the cause of death from the registrar of deaths or similar authority
Statement by the person who prepared the remains, certified by an appropriate authority, describing the preparation and confirming the coffin holds only the body and clothing
Transit permit stating name, age and sex (or a permit also naming cause of death, embalmer, coroner and public health officer)
coffin: Impervious coffin: a container hermetically sealed by gasket or by soldered/welded metal, or a plastic container sealed by heat or adhesive. No official witnessing of the sealing is described.
embalming: Proper embalming, or thorough washing and disinfection with packing and a disinfectant-soaked sheet, before shipment.
consular: No legalisation step is set out in the regulations. Ask the Grenada mission in the country of death whether documents must be authenticated.
arrival: Documents must accompany the shipment; customs and health clearance at the port of entry; the local funeral home collects. No legal burial deadline found.
pouch: The regulations allow a properly embalmed body in an air disaster bag or heat/adhesive-sealed plastic container; carriers usually still require a rigid outer container.
private_aviation: No private-flight rules found. Land at an airport of entry with customs and health officers and keep the documents with the remains.
export: Leaving Grenada: the death certificate (English, with cause of death) is issued by the Registrar General's Department, usually within a few days. Post-mortems usually take place 2-3 days after the body reaches the mortuary. The local funeral director provides the certificate of embalming and permission to transfer the remains. One crematorium operates on the island.

name: Trinidad and Tobago
summary: Importing a body requires prior approval from the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Homeland Security, obtained by the Ministry of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs after a Trinidad and Tobago mission certifies the original documents; Customs then clears the casket. For non-nationals, the family must first obtain approval from the Ministry of Homeland Security.
documents: Letter from the competent authority at the place of death confirming the documents are authentic
Original death certificate, apostilled or authenticated in the country of death
Original non-contagious disease letter from the coroner, doctor or hospital
Original permit to dispose of or transport human remains
Original embalming certificate from the funeral home abroad
Deceased's Trinidad and Tobago passport (or other passport); otherwise treated as a non-national
English translations by a registered translator, apostilled or authenticated, if needed
Non-nationals: letter to the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Homeland Security, explaining ties to Trinidad and Tobago
Fee set by the processing mission
coffin: The handbook does not set casket specifications; an embalming certificate is required. Airlines generally require a sealed casket in an outer case. Confirm with the receiving funeral home.
embalming: Required: an original embalming certificate from the funeral home abroad.
consular: The nearest Trinidad and Tobago mission (or honorary consul, or the local foreign ministry where there is none) certifies the original documents and sends them to the Consular Affairs Division in Port of Spain, which obtains the Ministry of Health and Ministry of Homeland Security approvals. Do not book confirmed flights before approval.
arrival: After approval, the Ministry of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs issues a letter to the Customs and Excise Division; the local funeral home collects it and obtains customs clearance (a no-objection document). The local funeral home collects the casket. No legal burial deadline found.
private_aviation: Approvals must be in hand before the flight is confirmed; most airlines require them and a private operator should too. The casket clears through the Customs and Excise Division at the port of entry with the receiving funeral home.
private_jet_note: Do not fly before Health and Homeland Security approvals are granted.
export: Leaving Trinidad and Tobago: register the death with the District Registrar (certificate usually within a week, longer if police investigate). The UK guidance lists the death certificate, permission to remove the body issued by a coroner, the passport and a letter confirming embalming and sealing of the coffin. The Consular Affairs Division may authenticate or apostille the death certificate. Post-mortems usually take place within 2-3 days.
